projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Virginia J. Bondra was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of Virginia J. Bondra. Mrs. Bondra was on the home front during World War II. She was a student and worked summers at a clothing factory making uniforms for the Navy. I'm Thom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mrs. Bondra's home in Mentor, Ohio, on December 15th, 2004. Virginia was 76 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I was born in 1928, January 8th, and I'll soon be 77 in January.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that means that you were almost 14 when the Japanese --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I was still in school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I was still in school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were still in school?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Pretty young.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before the attack on Pearl Harbor, did you follow the war news at all? In school?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I don't even remember that. We used to give reports on different generals, you know, things like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. What are your memories of the -- the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor, December 7th?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: My memories were it was the first time I saw my father cry when President Roosevelt gave the news that we would declare war on the Japanese. We were all very devastated.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How did you hear the news? Did you hear it listening --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: On the -- on the radio. We didn't have TV in those days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yeah. We were devastated.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, how did you react when you heard that news? Obviously you were pretty young, but --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Well, we all cried because we saw our parents crying.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: It was sad.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any brother -- older brothers at that time?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I had older -- well, my older brother died when he was 23. Pneumonia. And I had another older brother, but he was too young to go in the service. He was an albino, actually. And he couldn't have gone in the service. He had poor eyesight.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So your father crying was mostly -- not necessarily because he was going to have any sons going off to war?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: No. It was just very sad because we had heard all the boys, the young men, who were killed on the battleships in Pearl Harbor. And everybody there was running in different directions. They didn't know what to do. They were running to their posts and airplanes, whatever. They -- they just didn't know how to react.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, how long after that were you able to see any kind of the newsreel footage of what had happened there?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: The only newsreel footage we saw was in the theaters when we went to a movie. And we used to bring scrap metal or cans, and we'd get in the movies free. They needed scrap metal and they -- the USA needed scrap fat. My mother used to scrap fat, you know, in a can. She'd save it, and we'd bring it to a certain place. Sugar was rationed. Each member of the family would get one pound of sugar a week. And I always had time to bake because we had sugar. Things were -- different things were rationed. We couldn't buy nylons because it was needed. Nylon was needed for parachutes. So we'd -- we'd -- my older sisters would paint their legs with a certain makeup that came out in place of nylons.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So is that when --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: It was makeup for legs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Is that when they would put a line down the back of the leg?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: That's true. Some women did that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So it would look like they --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: They -- they painted a eyebrow pencil line down the back of their leg so it would look like real nylons. And we would write V-mail. I had brother -- brothers-in-law in the service. We -- we'd write V-mail to them. It was called V-mail. Victory mail. And the envelopes were real small. And it was like parchment paper. And we kept up their morale by writing V-mail. And it would go to a certain place, and they would distribute it to the troops wherever. We couldn't put their address on because they were moved around a lot and we didn't want the enemy to know. There were a lot of secrets. They would say "zip your lip was the" -- was the word of the days then. "Zip your lip" because we didn't want the enemy to get information.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what kinds of things would you write, when you did write?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Just little kid stuff like "how are you," and "I'm praying for." Things like that. "I hope you're getting along good and you're not getting too cold or hungry." Just things like that. And we had victory gardens because we couldn't buy everything anymore. So my father would have a garden, you know, and fruit trees. And we ate a lot of things; lettuce, tomatoes, vegetables, you know, from the garden. And, let's see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the rationing much of a problem as far as your problems_?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I didn't notice it because I was so young. I -- we didn't go hungry or anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because you couldn't get a lot of meat, right?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yeah. I think things like that were rationed, but I don't remember too well about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. And you didn't drive. So the probably rationing of tires really wouldn't -- something you think about, right?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Right. My father never drove. He took the streetcar or bus later on. They ditched the streetcars and we rode buses.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, what did you father do?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: My father was a custom tailor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did your parents get involved in the -- the war effort too?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not really?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, in school, did they -- they encourage you to do all this stuff; scrap drives and all this?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes. Yes. I think that's where we heard a lot of this. Now, we had practice blackouts where we had to keep the lights off. They'd -- the signal was a siren. We had to shut all the lights. You couldn't light candles or anything because if the war ever came to Cleveland, the enemy would see the sparks or the lights, you know. So it was a complete blackout. Yeah, there were certain rations. I -- I don't remember if meat was rationed, but probably it was. Old metal cans. We'd get in the movies free if we brought the metal cans in and metal --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did they -- what did they use the fat for that they collected?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I don't know. I couldn't tell you. I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I thought it was some kind of lubrication for machines --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Maybe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- or weapons, or whatever?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Maybe. Maybe they used grease for things like that, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And then maybe --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Maybe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- possibly dried and used as gunpowder or something. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I -- I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: These are just things I --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: That could be. That could be gunpowder.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Used as part of that.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I know there were canteen dances -- the USO canteens -- where the soldiers, when they would come home on furlough, they would go there and have doughnuts and coffee; dance with the girls there. They'd get a meal. Things like that. And the Red Cross helped them a lot with things like that too. My sister, Louise, was a WAC: Women's Army Auxiliary Army Corps. Her husband died when he was very young, and she'd cry all the time, so she joined the service. And all I remember was we used to write to her. She was stationed at Camp Adaberry in Indiana, or something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: And she went to New Guinea. And they had to take things -- they had to take certain pills so they wouldn't get malaria. That's all I remember about it. And she died pretty young. She had an aneurysm. And she'd come home on furlough. And there were a lot of soldiers walking in Cleveland going to theaters, restaurants, and things like that. And I'd be -- we'd go downtown sometimes. And the soldiers would all be friendly. "Hey soldier," they'd say, "Could I take you to a movie," or something like that, you know. But we never went with them. But they were all very friendly. And those days, the soldiers who came home, they always suggested to them that they should keep their uniforms on. They don't do that anymore. But you would see -- you would know them because they had Navy uniforms on or Army uniforms, you know. And -- and it was prevalent to see them downtown near the public square, you know, where there were theaters and restaurants. And it was a very patriotic time. I don't know if we're that patriotic anymore. We're -- people have a lot of criticism for wars now. But it was -- I remember after the World War II everybody was out of their house and streetcars were going by with people hanging out. And they'd say, "Hi. Yeah." You know, everyone was cheering. It was so beautiful. If you went on the main street everyone was there congratulating everybody, you know, kissing the soldiers, sailors, whoever was there. It was -- it was a thrilling time when the war ended. But it was a -- a very -- it was an evil war. Very bad. Germany, with all the things they did to the Jews, it was horrible.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you first hear about that -- what they had done?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I -- I really don't -

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember, exactly?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: -- remember. No. I was still in school and I saw pictures in a "Life" magazine about the Jewish prisoners. And they were real skinny and starving in these camps that the Germans -- Germany had them in. People from Poland. And they captured people from many nations. It was so evil. I couldn't believe it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news about the D-Day landings?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yeah. I remember that, but not -- just vaguely.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just vaguely remember?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there ever a point -- and then maybe you were too young to have appreciated that -- but ever a point that you thought that the war was going badly and that we might not win?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: No, not really. I was so young. I -- there's a lot I don't remember. We were afraid that we wouldn't win -- I'll say that -- because the enemies were very aggressive. You could see how it started. I mean, it was very aggressive. A lot of nerve they had, huh? I'm afraid that's all the information I -- I have here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I'll try to ask you a few questions.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: See if it jogs your memory about anything.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you follow the war news during the war? Did you follow it at all, either in magazines --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: On the radio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: On the radio?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: On the radio we did. Yes. I think I covered everything here. What else did you want to ask?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, do you have any specific memories of the day FDR died?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: The next day we went to school. Yes. And everybody knew about it. The teacher would ask us questions about it and answer questions about it. I remember that. And I do remember that FDR said -- the teacher asked us, What would you remember him by? And I raised my hand, and I said that the President said, "We have nothing to fear but fear itself." I remembered that. That's what he said. And I suppose he was encouraging us not to be afraid and just go forward, fight this battle to win.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you know much about Truman as the new President?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Some people complained about him, but what my family thought he was -- he was a good man. And some people would say, He's only President because FDR died. But he did a wonderful job. And he -- he had a sign on his desk. I remember that -- hearing about that -- that "the buck stops here." He was a good man. He'd get up real early in the morning and walk with his cane or umbrella, you know, Truman. I thought he was a good man. And he and his wife, Bess, were very close. And their daughter -- she -- the daughter was a pianist, a concert pianist. And -- and they were a close family. I thought he was a good President. And we didn't hear many complaints, as many as we do today about the Presidents.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news about the atomic bombs being dropped?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes, I do. And the thing about that that I remember -- I was happy they dropped the atomic bomb because that's what brought the war to the end. And I remember that the Japanese, Churchill, Roosevelt, were -- the Japanese President too -- they were talking peace. I forget where. They were all talking peace, and behind our back, the Japanese bombed us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh. Right. Right.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: While they were talking peace.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: While they were__.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: That's what made be angry. It was so sneaky, you know?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. There were Japanese diplomats in Washington at the time --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- of Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: And -- and they -- they snuck up on us and did this dastardly deed. And we were very angry about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not long after that they were moving the Japanese into the internment camps in America.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Oh, I remember that. Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction of people to that?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: We knew a Japanese boy in the neighborhood, and their house was empty and all the shades were down. I forget his name.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was he sent to one of those camps?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes. He and his family. And yes, that wasn't fair, but the United States didn't know what to do. We didn't know who the enemy was. It could have been right in our city, and that's why they did that. There was a reason for that. I know it wasn't nice, but it's wartime, you know?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing about any incidents of sabotage in the Cleveland area, or spying?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: There was a lot of spying, and that -- that's why they interned these people in different camps. There -- I heard about spying. We didn't know of a special incidence, but there was spying all over. What I heard, anyway. I was just a kid, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And I've heard that there were groups of -- before Pearl Harbor, anyway -- there were groups of pro-German supporters in particular in this, in the Cleveland area.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Pro-German supporters?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And I had heard some of that. I think they probably went underground after the war started, or changed their mind?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Probably. Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you don't remember anybody?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: No, I don't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there anybody -- do you remember anybody in the neighborhood who opposed the war?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I couldn't tell you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But like you said, it was a patriotic time, so --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Right. And a lot of the young boys went and were killed. It was -- it was sad.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any young boys from your neighborhood die in the war?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes. The butcher's son died. And my sister, who was a WAC, went and talked to the father. And he was crying. It was real sad. I was with my sister. She was a servicewoman. And, you know, it was just so sad. You know, they hugged and talked, and the father was crying, of course.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A lot of stars in the window? That sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes. There were stars in the window. And even today -- not today. Maybe the Gold Star Mothers are all gone now. But when there was a parade, we'd go up the corner -- maybe it was 20 years ago -- where the parade started on the corner here. And I'd always go to the -- the car where the Gold Star Mothers were and say "hello" to them. That was sad. I did -- I particularly loved the Gold Star Mothers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. What part of Cleveland were you living in back then?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: It was off of Kinsman.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: 125th Street and Kinsman. It's all changed now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you see many USO shows, or anything? Did they -- get a chance to go with your sister to any of those in Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: No. I didn't see those. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They didn't do a lot of entertaining in the Cleveland area for servicemen?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: They did, but, you know, I was pretty young. And we were sheltered, you know. We were young girls, my younger sister and I. We were sheltered. We didn't -- we didn't get out that much. We weren't allowed, you know. When I was a little older I was able to go downtown by myself and that was kind of thrilling. I -- I would go to the May Company, Higbee's, Haley's. You know, places like that. Tailor -- there were a lot of department stores in those days. There was Bailey Department Store, William Tailors, you know, and the ones I mentioned previous to this. It's so changed now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Now, you mentioned the celebrations when the war ended on V-J Day. Do you remember V-E Day in May when victory over --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- Germany --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes. I remember that too. It was -- people were shouting with glee, and they were real happy, you know. When we heard that we'd take to the streets and go on the main street and talk to everybody. Crowds would gather. And they have parts about prewar and during World War II on one of the channels on television. The P --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. One of the -- like the history channels, or something --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yeah. The history channels. It was Channel 10 when --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh. PBS.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They did something on that, right?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: They have that -- last week my daughter called me and she said that they're talking about Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were 17 then, probably, when the war ended. Did any of your classmates lie about their age and try to get in the service --

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes. There was a lot of that. And I did hear of one boy who played the bugle. He was about 15. And he lied about his age, and he was able to get in. And he'd play Reveille and things like that. They didn't check on their ages. They just accepted them. Maybe he said he was 18. He'd play Reveille and things with the bugle, whatever was required, you know. I heard about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So if he looked old enough, they -- they went with it. They really didn't check it, huh?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Right. And every day I'd look in the Cleveland Press. There was a strip of young men who went into the service, and they'd always show them every day in the paper. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were getting the news, either from the paper or the newsreels, did you think you were getting an accurate picture of the war, or did you think you were getting kind of an optimistic picture of the way things were going?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: No. Because a lot of it wasn't real nice. And the newsreels in the movie theaters -- we'd see the newsreels. And they were in black and white. I thought they were authentic. Our photographers would be there. Do you -- did you ever hear of Ernie Pyle?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: He was a war correspondent. We used to read his article every day. And he was killed along with the young men.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was killed in Okinawa, right?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: It was real sad.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Toward the end of the war, right?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I don't remember where, but you say it's Okinawa. He was a wonderful newsman. He gave accounts of different names and different lives and what was going on over there in the places. He traveled around to different places and gave the news very accurately. He was a wonderful man. We loved his articles. We were very sad when he was killed. Sad.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, we talked about the Japanese. Was there much suspicion or mistrust of the German population? A lot of German folks in the Cleveland area. Any mistrust of them?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Well, I worked in a factory during the summers, you know. And these women were arguing. One was Jewish and one was German. And they were both defending their cause. They -- they got into it. It was a men's clothing factory. I used to work on Navy officers' uniforms. We were sewing in the factory. And these women got into a big argument because one was Jewish and one was German. And the German lady was defending her country, which is understandable. But the poor Jewish lady had good reason to argue too. Her people were being starved to death, put in death camps. And it was all so horrible. How could you do that to people?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there mostly women working in that factory?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Women where I was. Yes. They were women.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did a lot of them continue to work after the war, then?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Yes, they did. Because they also made men's suits. During the war it was Navy uniforms. And, as I said, I worked on Navy officers' uniforms. After the war they made regular men's suits.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that a job that men had done before the war?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You don't know for sure? Well, you weren't there.

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: No. No, I wasn't there. I was there for the summers because I was still in school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you continue working after?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Well, after I graduated high school I worked at the telephone company. 750 Hearing Road. After that I got married and had a family. And I didn't work after that. I did go back to the telephone company in Painesville some years later, you know. But I didn't retire from there. I had a big family. I had six children.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: Uh-huh. And I have 13 grandchildren.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. When you think about the war years, does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nothing jumps out at you?

sp.speaker: Virginia J. Bondra
sp.p: No. No. I wish I could remember more things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No. That's fine. This is very good.
